title: Money Mastery
tagline: Read a paycheck, budget, build credit, dodge scams and start investing.
description: Understand exactly where your paycheck goes, build a budget you can actually keep, and set up the bank accounts and emergency fund that keep small problems small. You will learn how credit scores and interest really work, how to get out of debt, and how to start investing in index funds and retirement accounts while spotting scams before they cost you.

units.title: Paychecks and Taxes
units.description: Where your gross pay goes before it reaches your account, and how income tax really works.

levels.title: Decode Your Paycheck
levels.summary: Gross vs net pay, FICA, withholding and the W-4.

steps.title: Gross pay vs net pay
steps.body:
**Gross pay** is what you earned: hours x hourly rate, or your salary divided by pay periods.

**Net pay** (take-home pay) is what actually lands in your bank account after deductions.

The usual deductions:
- **Federal income tax** withholding
- **State and local income tax** (some states have none)
- **FICA**: Social Security and Medicare
- Benefits you chose: health insurance, 401(k) contributions

> Always budget with **net** pay. A $20/hour job does not put $20/hour in your pocket.

steps.prompt: You earn $18/hour, work 30 hours a week, and get paid every two weeks (biweekly). What is your **gross** pay per paycheck?
steps.explain: $18 x 30 hours = $540 per week. Biweekly means two weeks per check: $540 x 2 = **$1,080** gross.

steps.title: FICA: the tax almost everyone pays
steps.body:
**FICA** funds Social Security and Medicare. For employees in 2026:
- **Social Security: 6.2%** of wages, up to a yearly wage cap of $184,500
- **Medicare: 1.45%** of all wages

Together that is **7.65%**, taken from every paycheck. Your employer pays a matching 7.65% on top.

Unlike income tax, FICA has no standard deduction: it starts with your first dollar. That is why even a small part-time check shows FICA.

> If you are self-employed, you pay both halves: 15.3%.

steps.prompt: Your gross pay this check is $1,080. How much is withheld for FICA (7.65%)? Round to the cent.

steps.title: The W-4 controls your withholding
steps.body:
When you start a job you fill out **Form W-4**. It tells your employer how much federal income tax to hold back from each check.

- Most single people with one job just fill in **Step 1** (name, filing status) and **Step 5** (sign).
- **Step 2** is for multiple jobs. If you have two jobs and skip it, each employer withholds too little and you can owe at tax time.
- Steps 3-4 are for dependents and extra adjustments.

Withholding is a **prepayment**. Too much means a refund next spring; too little means a bill.

steps.prompt: Match each paycheck term to its meaning.
pairs: Total earned before anything is taken out
What actually reaches your bank account
Social Security + Medicare tax, 7.65% for employees
Form that sets your federal income tax withholding
The statement listing each deduction for one pay period
steps.explain: Read your pay stub every time: it shows gross pay, each deduction and net pay, so you catch mistakes like missing hours.

steps.prompt: Federal law requires overtime of 1.5x your regular rate for hours over 40 in a week for most hourly workers. You make $16/hour and work 45 hours. What is your gross pay for the week?
steps.explain: 40 x $16 = $640. Overtime rate = $16 x 1.5 = $24, and 5 x $24 = $120. Total **$760**. Check your stub to make sure overtime was paid.

steps.prompt: You just took a second part-time job. Your first job already withholds federal tax based on a W-4 where you only filled out Step 1. What do you do with the new W-4?

options.text: Fill out Step 2 (multiple jobs) on the W-4s, for example using the IRS Tax Withholding Estimator, so enough tax is withheld overall.
options.feedback: Right. Each employer only sees its own paycheck, so without Step 2 both withhold as if they were your only job.

options.text: Fill out the new W-4 exactly like the first one; withholding adds up automatically.
options.feedback: Each employer withholds as if it were your only job, so the combined withholding comes out too low and you may owe in April.

options.text: Write 'exempt' so you get bigger paychecks now.
options.feedback: Exempt is only for people who owed no federal income tax last year and expect to owe none this year. Claiming it wrongly means a big bill, and possibly penalties, later.

options.text: Skip the W-4; it is optional.
options.feedback: Without a W-4 your employer withholds as if you were single with no adjustments. It is better to fill it out correctly.

steps.explain: Withholding should roughly match the tax you will owe for the whole year. The IRS Tax Withholding Estimator (free on irs.gov) does the math for multiple jobs.

steps.prompt: Contributions to a traditional 401(k) usually come out before federal income tax is calculated, which lowers your income tax withholding.
steps.explain: Traditional 401(k) contributions are pre-tax for income tax (though FICA still applies). So putting $100 in might only shrink your take-home by about $80-90.

steps.prompt: Pull up your most recent pay stub (or a family member's, with permission). Write down gross pay, each deduction, and net pay. What percent of gross did you actually take home?
steps.placeholder: Gross: $___  Fed tax: $___  State: $___  FICA: $___  Net: $___  Net / Gross = ___%

levels.title: Tax Brackets Are Marginal
levels.summary: Why a raise never lowers your take-home pay, and deductions vs credits.

steps.title: Taxable income comes first
steps.body:
Federal income tax is not charged on every dollar you earn. First you subtract deductions.

Most people take the **standard deduction**. For tax year 2026 it is **$16,100** for a single filer ($32,200 married filing jointly). It changes every year with inflation.

> **Taxable income = income - deductions**

So a single person earning $16,100 or less in 2026 owes no federal income tax at all (FICA still applies).

steps.prompt: In 2026 you are single, earn a $40,000 salary and take the standard deduction of $16,100. What is your taxable income?

steps.title: Brackets fill up like buckets
steps.body:
Tax rates are **marginal**: each rate applies only to the dollars inside that bracket. 2026 brackets for a single filer start like this:

- **10%** on taxable income up to $12,400
- **12%** on the part from $12,400 to $50,400
- **22%** on the part from $50,400 to $105,700
- then 24%, 32%, 35%, 37% higher up

Your first $12,400 is always taxed at 10%, no matter how much you earn. Only dollars that spill into the next bucket get the next rate.

steps.prompt: Your 2026 taxable income is $23,900 (single). Using 10% up to $12,400 and 12% above that, what is your federal income tax?
steps.explain: 10% x $12,400 = $1,240. The rest is $23,900 - $12,400 = $11,500, and 12% x $11,500 = $1,380. Total **$2,620**. That is only about 6.6% of the $40,000 salary: your **effective rate**.

steps.prompt: Your taxable income is $50,000 and a raise would push it to $51,000, crossing into the 22% bracket. What happens?
options: All $51,000 is now taxed at 22%, so you could take home less
Only the $600 above $50,400 is taxed at 22%; the rest is taxed exactly as before
Nothing changes until you pass $60,000
Your whole raise is taxed at 22%, including the part under $50,400
steps.explain: Marginal brackets mean only dollars above $50,400 get 22%. Of the $1,000 raise, $400 is taxed at 12% ($48) and $600 at 22% ($132): $180 more federal income tax. You still keep most of the raise. A raise never lowers your take-home from brackets alone.

steps.title: Deductions vs credits
steps.body:
Two tools lower your tax, and they are not equal.

- A **deduction** lowers your *taxable income*. A $1,000 deduction in the 12% bracket saves $120.
- A **credit** lowers your *tax bill* dollar for dollar. A $1,000 credit saves $1,000.

Common credits for young adults include education credits (like the American Opportunity Tax Credit for college costs) and the Earned Income Tax Credit for lower-income workers. Tax software asks the questions that find them.

steps.prompt: You are in the 12% bracket. How much tax does a $500 deduction save you?
steps.explain: A deduction removes $500 of taxable income, which would have been taxed at 12%: $500 x 0.12 = **$60**. A $500 *credit* would have saved the full $500.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Rate on your last (highest) dollar of taxable income
Total tax divided by total income
Flat amount subtracted from income before tax
Dollar-for-dollar cut to the tax you owe
steps.explain: Your marginal rate tells you what a little extra income costs in tax; your effective rate tells you what share of all your income went to tax.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Taxable income = income - deductions (2026 single standard deduction: $16,100).
- Brackets are buckets: each rate hits only the dollars inside it.
- Taking a raise or extra shifts never lowers your take-home because of brackets.
- Credits beat deductions of the same size.

> Numbers change every year. Check the IRS's current figures when you file.

levels.title: Filing Your Tax Return
levels.summary: Forms, deadlines, free filing options and what a refund really is.

steps.title: What filing a return means
steps.body:
Each spring you file a **tax return** for the previous year. It compares the tax you actually owe with what was withheld from your paychecks.

- Withheld more than you owe: you get a **refund**.
- Withheld less: you **owe** the difference.

The deadline is usually **April 15**. For 2026 income, that is April 15, 2027.

Key forms arrive by about **January 31**:
- **W-2** from each employer (wages and withholding)
- **1099** forms for other income: freelance work, bank interest, investments

steps.prompt: Your W-2 shows $2,900 of federal income tax withheld. Your return shows you owe $2,620. What is your refund?
steps.explain: $2,900 withheld - $2,620 owed = **$280** refund. It is your own money coming back: you lent it to the government interest-free.

steps.prompt: A big tax refund means you got a good deal from the IRS.
steps.explain: A refund only means you overpaid during the year. A huge refund means smaller paychecks all year. Many people prefer to adjust their W-4 so they get a small refund or owe a little.

steps.title: Do you need to file?
steps.body:
A single person under 65 generally **must** file if gross income is above the standard deduction ($16,100 for 2026). If you had **self-employment** income of $400 or more, you must file even if you earned less.

But even when you don't have to, you often **should**: if tax was withheld, filing is the only way to get it back.

> All income counts, even cash tips, side gigs and freelance work with no 1099 form.

steps.prompt: You earned $6,000 at a summer job in 2026 and $310 in federal tax was withheld. You don't legally have to file. What should you do?

options.text: File a return anyway to get the $310 back.
options.feedback: Yes. With $6,000 of income you owe $0 federal income tax, so filing returns all $310 withheld.

options.text: Skip it: if you are not required to file, the IRS mails the money automatically.
options.feedback: The IRS does not refund withholding unless you file a return asking for it.

options.text: Wait and file all your returns together when you turn 25.
options.feedback: You generally have only 3 years from the due date to claim a refund. Waiting can forfeit it.

steps.explain: Filing is how you claim withheld tax back. Small refunds are still your money.

steps.title: Ways to file for free
steps.body:
- **IRS Free File** (irs.gov/freefile): brand-name software, free for people under an income limit.
- **VITA**: free in-person help from IRS-certified volunteers, usually for low-to-moderate income filers.
- Many paid apps have a free tier for simple returns, but watch for upsells.

Note: the IRS's own **Direct File** tool was not offered in the 2026 filing season.

> Keep copies of your return and its forms for at least 3 years.

steps.prompt: Put the steps of filing a simple return in order.
items: Collect your W-2s and 1099s (they arrive by about January 31)
Choose a filing method, like IRS Free File or a VITA site
Enter your income, withholding and deductions or credits
Review the numbers, then submit by April 15
Save a copy of the return and the forms for your records
steps.explain: Gather first, then file, then keep records. Filing electronically with direct deposit usually gets a refund to you fastest.

steps.prompt: You can't finish your return by April 15. What does filing an extension do?
options: Gives you more time to file AND more time to pay with no interest
Gives you more time to file the paperwork, but any tax owed is still due April 15
Cancels late penalties for the whole year
Only works if you are getting a refund
steps.explain: An extension (usually to October 15) is more time to *file*, not to *pay*. Estimate what you owe and pay it by April 15 to avoid interest and penalties.

steps.prompt: Write down where your W-2s will be sent (mail? employer portal?), which free filing method you will use, and a date in February when you will file.
steps.placeholder: My W-2 comes from... I'll file with... on (date)...

units.title: Budgeting and Banking
units.description: Give every dollar a job, pick the right accounts, and build a cushion for emergencies.

levels.title: The 50/30/20 Budget
levels.summary: A simple split of take-home pay into needs, wants and savings.

steps.title: A budget is a plan, not a punishment
steps.body:
A budget tells your money where to go *before* the month starts, instead of wondering where it went afterward.

The simplest starting point is **50/30/20**, based on your **take-home** pay:
- **50% needs**: rent, utilities, groceries, insurance, transportation, minimum debt payments
- **30% wants**: eating out, streaming, hobbies, upgrades
- **20% savings and extra debt payoff**: emergency fund, retirement, paying debt faster

It is a guideline. In a high-rent city needs may run higher; then trim wants first.

steps.prompt: Your monthly take-home pay is $2,800. Using 50/30/20, how much goes to **wants**?

steps.title: Need or want?
steps.body:
A **need** is something you must pay to live and work: a basic place to live, basic food, getting to your job, required insurance, minimum loan payments.

A **want** is the upgrade on top: the newer phone, the nicer apartment, takeout instead of groceries.

Many items are partly both. Basic groceries are a need; the energy drinks in the cart are a want. A phone plan is a need; the $40/month premium tier is mostly a want.

steps.prompt: Which of these are **needs** in a 50/30/20 budget? Select all that apply.
options: Rent for a basic apartment
Concert tickets
Car insurance required by law
A third streaming service
Minimum payment on a student loan
Basic groceries
steps.explain: Rent, legally required insurance, minimum debt payments and basic food are needs. Concerts and extra subscriptions are wants. Paying *more* than the minimum on debt counts toward the 20%.

steps.prompt: Take-home pay is $3,200/month. Your needs add up to $1,920. What percent of take-home pay is going to needs?
steps.explain: $1,920 / $3,200 = 0.60 = **60%**. That is 10 points over the 50% guideline, so wants or savings have to shrink, or you look for cheaper housing or transport.

steps.prompt: Your needs take 60% of take-home pay because rent is high. Your 30% wants include $250/month of takeout and $45 in subscriptions. What is the best first move?

options.text: Cut wants (cook more, drop unused subscriptions) so savings stays at about 20%.
options.feedback: Good. Wants are the easiest lever to pull this month, and it protects your savings habit.

options.text: Stop saving until you get a raise.
options.feedback: Raises often get absorbed by spending. Skipping savings leaves you exposed to the next emergency.

options.text: Put the gap on a credit card each month.
options.feedback: Borrowing to cover regular monthly costs grows a balance at 20%+ interest. That makes the problem worse.

steps.explain: When needs run high, trim wants first and keep at least some savings flowing. Longer-term fixes: a roommate, cheaper housing at lease renewal, or more income.

steps.prompt: You should build your 50/30/20 budget on your gross (before-tax) pay.
steps.explain: Use take-home (net) pay. Taxes come out before you ever see the money, so budgeting gross pay plans for money you don't have.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Start with take-home pay.
- Aim for about 50% needs, 30% wants, 20% savings and extra debt payoff.
- When needs run high, trim wants before cutting savings.
- Pay yourself first: set an automatic transfer to savings on payday so the 20% happens without willpower.

steps.prompt: Estimate your monthly take-home pay and list your needs and wants. What are your 50/30/20 dollar targets, and where are you over?
steps.placeholder: Take-home $___. Needs target $___ (actual $___). Wants target $___. Save $___.

levels.title: Zero-Based Budgeting
levels.summary: Give every dollar a job, plan for irregular costs and track spending.

steps.title: Every dollar gets a job
steps.body:
A **zero-based budget** assigns every dollar of income to a category until the leftover is **$0**. Zero does not mean you spend it all: savings and debt payoff are categories too.

> Income - all assigned categories = $0

Why it works: money with no job tends to disappear on small purchases. When every dollar has a label, you notice the moment you overspend in one category and must move money from another.

steps.prompt: Monthly income: $2,400. Assigned so far: rent $950, groceries $320, gas and car insurance $260, phone $45, subscriptions $25, emergency fund $300, fun money $200. How many dollars still need a job?
steps.explain: 950 + 320 + 260 + 45 + 25 + 300 + 200 = $2,100. $2,400 - $2,100 = **$300** left to assign, for example to a car-repair fund or extra debt payment.

steps.title: Sinking funds for 'surprise' bills
steps.body:
Many budget-breakers are not surprises at all: car registration, holiday gifts, annual subscriptions, new tires, back-to-school costs.

A **sinking fund** spreads them out: add up the yearly cost, divide by 12, and set that much aside every month.

> Example: $240 car registration / 12 = $20 per month.

When the bill arrives, the money is already waiting.

steps.prompt: You expect $180 for car registration and $600 for birthday and holiday gifts this year. How much should go into a sinking fund each month to cover both?
Put the monthly zero-based budgeting routine in order.
items: Write down the income you will actually receive this month
Assign money to fixed needs (rent, utilities, insurance)
Assign savings, debt payments and sinking funds
Assign variable spending (groceries, gas, fun) until $0 is left
Track spending during the month and move money between categories when you overspend
steps.explain: Plan with real income, cover essentials and savings early, then give the rest to flexible categories. Adjusting mid-month is part of the plan, not failure.

steps.prompt: Halfway through the month your grocery category is empty, but you have $60 left in fun money. Friends invite you out for $40. What do you do?

options.text: Move money from fun to groceries first, then decide whether anything is left for going out.
options.feedback: Exactly. Food comes first; you can still join for a cheaper hangout or skip this one.

options.text: Go out and put groceries on a credit card.
options.feedback: That turns a budget overspend into debt, and the budget stops telling the truth.

options.text: Give up on the budget because it didn't work this month.
options.feedback: Every budget needs adjusting. Moving money between categories is the system working.

steps.explain: When one category runs out, you move money from another. Needs win over wants.

steps.prompt: Which tracking method is most likely to stick for a busy person?
options: Saving every paper receipt and adding them up once a year
Checking your bank app or budgeting app for 5 minutes a few times a week and labeling transactions
Only looking at your balance when a card gets declined
Guessing at the end of the month
steps.explain: Short, frequent check-ins catch problems while you can still fix them. Most banks and budgeting apps can categorize transactions automatically.

steps.prompt: In a zero-based budget, reaching $0 means you must spend all your income by the end of the month.
steps.explain: Savings, investing and debt payoff are categories. $0 means every dollar has a job, and some of those jobs are 'stay saved'.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Income - assignments = $0, with savings as an assignment.
- Use sinking funds for predictable yearly costs: yearly total / 12.
- Check spending a few times a week.
- Overspent? Move money from another category instead of reaching for a credit card.

levels.title: Bank Accounts and Your Emergency Fund
levels.summary: Checking, savings, high-yield savings, overdraft and your safety cushion.

steps.title: Three accounts, three jobs
steps.body:
- **Checking**: for spending. Debit card, bill pay, direct deposit. Pays little or no interest.
- **Savings**: for money you are not spending this month.
- **High-yield savings account (HYSA)**: a savings account, often at an online bank, that pays much more interest than a typical savings account. Rates change with the economy.

Check that the bank is **FDIC-insured** (credit unions: **NCUA**). Deposits are protected up to **$250,000** per depositor, per bank, per ownership category if the bank fails.

steps.prompt: You keep $5,000 in savings. A HYSA pays 3.5% APY and your current savings account pays 0.01%. Roughly how much more interest would the HYSA earn in a year? (Ignore the tiny 0.01% interest.)
steps.explain: $5,000 x 0.035 = **$175** per year, versus about $0.50 at 0.01%. Same money, same safety (if FDIC-insured), much more interest. Rates are an example; they move over time.

steps.title: Overdrafts and how to avoid fees
steps.body:
An **overdraft** happens when you spend more than is in your checking account. The bank may cover it and charge a fee, often around $25-$35 per item at banks that still charge one.

Protect yourself:
- For **debit card and ATM** purchases, banks can only charge overdraft fees if you **opted in**. You can opt out; the purchase is simply declined.
- Turn on **low-balance alerts** in your bank app.
- Link savings as backup, or pick a bank with no overdraft fees.
- Keep a small buffer (like $100) you treat as zero.

steps.prompt: Your checking account has $40. You buy $55 of groceries with your debit card. You never opted in to overdraft coverage for debit purchases. What most likely happens?

options.text: The card is declined at the register, and no overdraft fee is charged.
options.feedback: Right. Without opt-in, the bank can't charge an overdraft fee on a one-time debit card purchase; it usually just declines it.

options.text: The purchase goes through and you are charged a $35 overdraft fee.
options.feedback: That can happen if you opted in. Without opt-in, the bank can't charge that fee on a one-time debit purchase.

options.text: Your account is immediately closed.
options.feedback: One declined purchase does not close an account.

steps.explain: Opt-in rules apply to one-time debit card and ATM transactions. Checks and automatic bill payments can still overdraft, so alerts and a buffer still matter.

steps.title: The emergency fund
steps.body:
An **emergency fund** is cash set aside for true surprises: a car repair, a medical bill, losing your job. It turns an emergency into an inconvenience instead of credit card debt.

A common plan:
1. Build a **starter fund** of about $1,000 fast.
2. Grow it to **3-6 months of essential expenses** (needs, not wants).

Keep it in a separate savings account or HYSA: easy to reach in a day or two, but not on your debit card.

steps.prompt: Your essential expenses (rent, food, utilities, insurance, transport, minimum debt payments) are $1,800 per month. What is a **3-month** emergency fund?
steps.explain: $1,800 x 3 = **$5,400**. A 6-month fund would be $10,800. Count only essentials, since you would cut wants in a real emergency.

steps.prompt: Which of these are good uses of an emergency fund? Select all that apply.
options: Your car's alternator dies and you need it for work
A sale on a new gaming console
Rent after an unexpected layoff
An urgent care bill after a sprained ankle
Concert tickets that are about to sell out
steps.explain: Emergencies are unexpected, necessary and urgent. Sales and tickets are wants; plan for them with a sinking fund instead.

steps.prompt: Match each account to its best job.
pairs: Saving monthly for a known future cost
Card is declined instead of charging a fee
steps.explain: Separate accounts make it obvious which money is for spending and which is off-limits.

steps.prompt: What are your essential monthly expenses? Write your starter and 3-month emergency fund targets and the automatic transfer you'll set up to reach them.
steps.placeholder: Essentials $___/mo. Starter goal $1,000 by ___. 3-month goal $___. Auto-transfer $___ every payday.

units.title: Credit and Debt
units.description: How credit scores work, how to build credit from zero, and how to escape interest traps.

levels.title: How Credit Scores Work
levels.summary: The five FICO factors, utilization and checking your credit report.

steps.title: Why your score matters
steps.body:
A **credit score** is a 3-digit number (usually **300-850** for FICO) that predicts how likely you are to repay borrowed money. Lenders, landlords, and insurers in most states may use your credit, and a better record can mean:
- Lower interest on car loans and mortgages
- Approval for an apartment
- Lower deposits for utilities and phone plans

Your score comes from your **credit report**: the record of your accounts and payments kept by Equifax, Experian and TransUnion. It does not include your income, age or bank balance.

steps.title: The five FICO factors
steps.body:
FICO says scores weigh these, for the general population:
- **Payment history: 35%**. Do you pay on time?
- **Amounts owed: 30%**. Especially **utilization**: how much of your credit limits you are using.
- **Length of credit history: 15%**. Age of your oldest and average accounts.
- **New credit: 10%**. Recent applications and new accounts.
- **Credit mix: 10%**. Cards and loans together.

> Two-thirds of the score is just paying on time and keeping balances low.

steps.prompt: Match each FICO factor to its weight.
steps.explain: Payment history and amounts owed together make up 65% of a FICO score.

steps.prompt: You have one card with a $2,000 limit and your statement shows a $600 balance. What is your credit utilization?
steps.explain: $600 / $2,000 = 0.30 = **30%**. Lower is better. Many people aim for under 30%, and people with top scores often stay under 10%.

steps.prompt: Which action would usually help your score the **most** over the next year?
options: Opening three new store cards to get more available credit
Paying every bill on time and keeping card balances low
Closing your oldest credit card
Checking your own score every day
steps.explain: On-time payments (35%) and low utilization (30%) are the biggest factors. New applications can lower your score a bit, closing your oldest card can shorten your history, and checking your own score is a soft inquiry with no effect.

steps.title: Check your credit report for free
steps.body:
You can get free credit reports from all three bureaus **every week** at **AnnualCreditReport.com**, the only official site. Lookalike sites may try to sell you something.

Look for:
- Accounts you don't recognize (possible identity theft)
- Late payments that were actually on time
- Wrong personal info

Dispute errors directly with the bureau that shows them. A **credit freeze** is free and blocks new accounts being opened in your name.

steps.prompt: A payment that is 5 days late will show up as a late payment on your credit report.
steps.explain: You may pay a late fee, but lenders generally report a payment as late to the bureaus once it is **30 days** past due. Still, pay on time every time: set up autopay for at least the minimum.

steps.prompt: On your free credit report you find a credit card you never opened, with a $900 balance. What do you do first?

options.text: Freeze your credit at all three bureaus, report it at IdentityTheft.gov, and dispute the account with the bureaus and the lender.
options.feedback: Correct. The freeze stops more fraud, and IdentityTheft.gov gives you a recovery plan and report to use with lenders.

options.text: Pay the $900 so it doesn't hurt your score.
options.feedback: You are not responsible for fraudulent accounts. Paying it doesn't fix the identity theft.

options.text: Ignore it; the bureau will catch it.
options.feedback: Bureaus don't know which accounts are yours. Unreported fraud can grow and damage your credit for years.

steps.explain: Spot it, freeze, report, dispute. Checking your report a few times a year is how you catch this early.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Scores run about 300-850 and come from your credit report.
- Pay on time (35%) and keep utilization low (30%).
- Pull your free reports at AnnualCreditReport.com and dispute errors.
- A credit freeze is free and is one of the best identity theft protections.

levels.title: Build Credit From Zero
levels.summary: First credit options and how to use a credit card without ever paying interest.

steps.title: The no-credit catch-22
steps.body:
With no history you have no score, and with no score it is hard to get approved. Starter options:
- **Secured credit card**: you put down a deposit (say $300) that becomes your limit. Use it lightly, pay in full, and many upgrade to a regular card later.
- **Student credit card**: for college students, with low limits.
- **Authorized user**: a parent adds you to their well-managed card, and its history can show on your report.
- **Credit-builder loan**: offered by many credit unions; you repay a small loan into savings.

Under 21, you need your own income or a co-signer to get a card.

steps.prompt: Your secured card has a $300 limit. You want to keep utilization under 10% when the statement closes. What is the highest statement balance you should let it show?
steps.explain: 10% x $300 = **$30**. One small recurring bill (like a phone or streaming bill) on autopay keeps the card active and utilization low.

steps.title: The grace period: how to never pay interest
steps.body:
Each month your card has a **statement balance** and a **due date**. If you pay the **full statement balance** by the due date, most cards charge **no interest** on purchases. That interest-free window is the **grace period**.

Pay only part of it, and interest starts on the leftover balance, usually at 20%+ APR. You also typically lose the grace period on new purchases until you pay in full again.

> Rule: only charge what is already in your checking account.

steps.prompt: Put the safe-credit-card routine in order.
items: Use the card for a planned purchase you already have cash for
Track the charge in your budget like it was debit
Get the statement and check it for mistakes or fraud
Pay the full statement balance by the due date (autopay)
Watch your score grow from on-time payments
steps.explain: Treat the card like a debit card with a delay. Autopay for the full statement balance means a busy week never turns into a late payment.

steps.prompt: Which credit card habit costs the most money?
options: Paying the full statement balance every month
Taking a cash advance from the card at an ATM
Using the card only for gas
Setting a low credit limit
steps.explain: Cash advances usually have a fee (often 3-5%), a higher APR, and no grace period: interest starts the same day. Avoid them.

steps.prompt: You've had your first credit card for 18 months, always paid in full. A store offers 20% off today if you open its store card. You don't need one. What do you do?

options.text: Skip it. The one-time discount isn't worth a hard inquiry, a new account, and the temptation of a high-APR card.
options.feedback: Good call. Store cards often have very high APRs, and the discount is usually small in dollars.

options.text: Open it to save 20%, and then close it right away.
options.feedback: You still take the hard inquiry and a new account; closing it right away doesn't undo those.

options.text: Open it and carry a balance so it builds credit faster.
options.feedback: Carrying a balance only costs interest. It does not build credit any faster than paying in full.

steps.explain: Apply for credit only when you need it. Each application is a hard inquiry, and new accounts lower your average account age.

steps.prompt: You need to carry a small balance month to month to build credit.
steps.explain: This is a myth. Your on-time payments and the statement balance being reported build your history. Paying in full builds credit and costs $0 in interest.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: What you owed when the billing cycle closed
Smallest payment that avoids a late fee
Window when paying in full means no interest
Card whose limit is backed by your cash deposit
steps.explain: Pay the statement balance, not just the minimum, to stay inside the grace period.

steps.prompt: Which starter option fits you best (secured card, student card, authorized user, credit-builder loan)? Write the one bill you'd put on it and how you'll set up autopay.
steps.placeholder: I'll start with... The only charge will be... Autopay: full statement balance on day...

levels.title: Interest Traps and Getting Out of Debt
levels.summary: APR, the minimum-payment trap, avalanche vs snowball, and student loan basics.

steps.title: APR in plain English
steps.body:
**APR** (annual percentage rate) is the yearly cost of borrowing. Credit cards charge it monthly: roughly **APR / 12** each month on your balance.

> 24% APR = about 2% per month.

On a $3,000 balance, 2% is about $60 of interest in one month. If your payment is only a little more than that, almost nothing goes to the actual debt.

steps.prompt: You owe $3,000 on a card with a 24% APR. About how much interest is added in the first month?
steps.explain: 24% / 12 = 2% per month. 2% x $3,000 = **$60**. A $60 payment would leave the balance exactly where it started.

steps.title: The minimum-payment trap
steps.body:
Minimum payments are set low so the debt lasts a long time. Same $3,000 at 24% APR, fixed payments, no new charges:

- **$100/month**: about **47 months** and about **$1,600 in interest**
- **$200/month**: about **19 months** and about **$600 in interest**

Doubling the payment cuts the time by more than half and saves about $1,000. Your statement includes a box showing how long the minimum would take. Read it once; it is motivating.

steps.prompt: Why does paying $200 instead of $100 per month save so much interest?
options: The bank gives a discount for larger payments
More of each payment goes to principal, so the balance that interest is charged on shrinks faster
Interest stops once you pay over $150
It only saves money because of the grace period
steps.explain: Interest is charged on the balance. A bigger payment knocks the balance down faster, so every following month's interest is smaller. That snowballs in your favor.

steps.title: Avalanche vs snowball
steps.body:
With several debts, pay the minimum on all of them, then put every extra dollar on one target:

- **Avalanche**: target the **highest interest rate** first. Saves the most money.
- **Snowball**: target the **smallest balance** first. Quick wins keep you motivated.

When the target is paid off, roll its whole payment into the next one. Both work far better than spreading extra money evenly. The best method is the one you will stick with.

steps.prompt: You have: Card A $400 at 27% APR, Card B $2,500 at 22% APR, Car loan $6,000 at 8% APR. You want to save the most interest. Where does your extra $150/month go?

options.text: Card A (27%), then Card B, then the car loan.
options.feedback: Correct for the avalanche method: highest APR first. Here Card A is also the smallest, so you get a quick win too.

options.text: The car loan, because it is the biggest.
options.feedback: The car loan has the lowest rate, so extra money there saves the least interest.

options.text: Split it evenly across all three.
options.feedback: Splitting slows everything down. Focusing on one target pays it off fastest.

steps.explain: Avalanche = highest APR first while paying minimums on the rest. In this case avalanche and snowball happen to agree on the first target.

steps.title: Student loan basics
steps.body:
- **Federal loans** (apply through the FAFSA) have fixed rates and protections like income-based repayment. For 2026-27, new undergraduate Direct Loans are **6.52%**.
- **Subsidized** loans: the government pays interest while you're in school at least half-time (need-based).
- **Unsubsidized** loans: interest builds from day one.
- **Private loans**: from banks, fewer protections. Use only after federal options.

A common rule of thumb: keep total borrowing below your expected first-year salary.

steps.prompt: You borrow a $5,500 unsubsidized loan at 6.52%. About how much interest builds up during one school year (simple interest)? Round to the nearest dollar.
steps.explain: $5,500 x 0.0652 = **$358.60**, about $359 in one year. Over four years of school that adds up, which is why borrowing less matters.

steps.prompt: List any debts you have (or expect to have) with balance and APR. Which would you target first with the avalanche method, and how much extra could you put on it each month?
steps.placeholder: Debt / balance / APR... First target: ... Extra per month: $...

units.title: Grow and Guard Your Money
units.description: Compound interest, index funds, retirement accounts, and protecting yourself from scams.

levels.title: Compound Interest and Time
levels.summary: Why starting early beats starting big.

steps.title: Interest on your interest
steps.body:
**Compound interest** means your earnings start earning too.

$1,000 growing 7% a year:
- Year 1: $1,000 + $70 = $1,070
- Year 2: $1,070 + $74.90 = $1,144.90

The growth each year gets bigger because the base gets bigger. The formula:

> Future value = Start x (1 + rate)^years

The 7% is an example, not a promise. Real investment returns go up and down from year to year.

steps.prompt: You invest $1,000 and it grows 7% per year, compounded yearly. What is it worth after 10 years? Round to the nearest dollar.
steps.explain: $1,000 x 1.07^10 = $1,000 x 1.967 = about **$1,967**. It nearly doubled without you adding a dollar.

steps.title: The rule of 72
steps.body:
Quick mental math: **72 / interest rate = years to double**.

- At 6%: 72 / 6 = about 12 years
- At 9%: 72 / 9 = about 8 years

It works in reverse too. Credit card debt at 24% doubles in about 72 / 24 = **3 years** if you don't pay it.

steps.prompt: Using the rule of 72, about how many years does money take to double at 8% per year?
steps.explain: 72 / 8 = **9 years**. So $5,000 at 8% becomes about $10,000 in 9 years and about $20,000 in 18.

steps.title: Time in the market beats timing
steps.body:
Two friends invest **$200 a month**, earning an assumed 7% a year:

- **Alex** starts at 22 and stops at 62 (40 years). Puts in $96,000. Ends with about **$525,000**.
- **Sam** starts at 32 and stops at 62 (30 years). Puts in $72,000. Ends with about **$244,000**.

Alex invested only $24,000 more but ended with more than **twice** as much. Those first 10 years got the longest time to compound.

Trying to jump in and out to dodge drops ("timing the market") usually means missing some of the best days.

steps.prompt: Why does Alex end up with more than twice as much as Sam?
options: Alex picked better stocks
Alex's early dollars had 10 extra years to compound, and growth is biggest at the end
Alex invested twice as much money
Sam paid higher taxes
steps.explain: Same return and same monthly amount; the only difference is time. Early contributions get the most doublings.

steps.prompt: Since you're young and don't earn much, it's better to wait until you can invest a large amount.
steps.explain: Small amounts started early often beat larger amounts started later. Even $25-$50 a month builds the habit and gets compounding started.

steps.prompt: Credit card debt at 18% APR left unpaid: using the rule of 72, about how many years until it doubles?
steps.explain: 72 / 18 = **4 years**. Compounding works against you on debt, which is why paying off high-interest debt usually comes before investing beyond an employer match.

steps.prompt: Pick a monthly amount you could invest starting now, even if it's small. Use the Investor.gov compound interest calculator to see what it could grow to by age 60 at 6-7%. Write the number down.
steps.placeholder: $___ per month from age ___ could grow to about $___ by 60.

levels.title: Index Funds and Retirement Accounts
levels.summary: Low-cost index funds, Roth IRA vs 401(k), and free money from an employer match.

steps.title: Index funds: own a slice of everything
steps.body:
A **stock** is a small piece of one company. Betting on one company is risky.

An **index fund** buys every company in an index. An S&P 500 index fund owns about 500 large US companies; a total market fund owns thousands. You get **diversification**: no single company can sink you.

Index funds just copy the index, so they are cheap. Their yearly fee, the **expense ratio**, is often under 0.1%. Most professional stock pickers fail to beat the index over long periods after fees.

steps.prompt: You have $10,000 in a fund with a 1% expense ratio. How much do you pay in fees per year? (A 0.04% index fund would charge $4.)
steps.explain: $10,000 x 0.01 = **$100 a year**, versus $4 at 0.04%. Over decades, high fees can eat tens of thousands of dollars of growth.

steps.title: Roth IRA vs 401(k)
steps.body:
These are **accounts**; inside them you pick investments like index funds.

- **401(k)**: through your employer, taken straight from your paycheck. 2026 limit: **$24,500** ($25,500 in 2027). *Traditional* = tax break now, taxed later.
- **Roth IRA**: you open it yourself at a brokerage. You pay tax now; growth and qualified withdrawals in retirement are **tax-free**. 2026 limit: **$7,500** (same for 2027), and you need earned income at least equal to what you put in.

Young people in low tax brackets often favor Roth: pay low tax now instead of possibly higher tax later.

steps.title: The employer match: free money
steps.body:
Many employers **match** your 401(k) contributions. A common formula: **50% match on up to 6% of salary**. Put in 6%, and your employer adds 3%.

Not taking the full match is turning down part of your pay.

Check **vesting**: some employers make you stay a certain number of years before their match is fully yours. Your own contributions are always yours.

steps.prompt: You earn $50,000. Your employer matches 50% of what you contribute, up to 6% of salary. You contribute 6%. How much does your employer add per year?
steps.explain: 6% of $50,000 = $3,000 from you. The match is 50% of that: **$1,500** free, an instant 50% return on your money before any market growth.

steps.prompt: Match each term to its meaning.
pairs: Fund that owns every company in a market index
Yearly fee as a percent of what you invest
Pay tax now, qualified retirement withdrawals tax-free
When employer contributions become fully yours
Spreading money across many investments to lower risk
steps.explain: Low-cost, diversified index funds inside tax-advantaged accounts are the core of most simple long-term plans.

steps.prompt: Here is one common order for where your next dollars go. Put it in order.
items: Build a starter emergency fund (about $1,000)
Contribute enough to the 401(k) to get the full employer match
Pay off high-interest debt like credit cards
Grow the emergency fund to 3-6 months of expenses
Contribute to a Roth IRA and more to the 401(k)
steps.explain: The starter fund stops new debt, the match is an instant 50-100% return, credit card interest (20%+) beats likely market returns, then you build security and long-term investing. Plans vary, but this order is widely recommended.

steps.prompt: Six months after you start investing in an index fund, the market drops 15% and your account is down. What do you do?

options.text: Keep investing on schedule. You are buying shares on sale, and you won't need the money for decades.
options.feedback: Right. Drops are normal; markets have recovered from every past decline, though how long it takes varies.

options.text: Sell everything to stop the losses, then buy back when it feels safe.
options.feedback: Selling locks in the loss, and 'feels safe' usually comes after prices have already recovered.

options.text: Move it all into one stock that is going up right now.
options.feedback: Chasing one hot stock removes your diversification and raises risk.

steps.explain: Money for long-term goals belongs in the market through ups and downs. Money you need within a few years (like an emergency fund) belongs in savings, not stocks.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Index funds give cheap, instant diversification. Check the expense ratio.
- Get the full employer match first: it's part of your pay.
- Roth IRA: tax now, tax-free later. 2026 limit $7,500.
- 401(k): 2026 limit $24,500.
- Stay invested through drops; keep short-term money in savings.

levels.title: Spot and Stop Scams
levels.summary: Red flags, common scams aimed at young adults, and what to do if you're hit.

steps.title: Scams are a big business
steps.body:
People reported losing about **$15.9 billion** to fraud in 2025, according to the FTC, a record. **Investment scams** caused the biggest losses, and **imposter scams** (someone pretending to be your bank, the government, a boss or a friend) were reported most. Losses from scams that started on social media keep climbing.

Scammers target young adults with fake jobs, fake online sellers and crypto 'opportunities'. Knowing the patterns is your best defense.

steps.prompt: Which are classic scam red flags? Select all that apply.
options: They demand payment by gift card, crypto, wire transfer or payment app
They create urgency: act in the next hour or your account is closed
They ask you to keep it secret from family or your bank
Your bank's app shows a monthly statement is ready
They promise guaranteed high returns with no risk
steps.explain: Unusual payment methods, pressure, secrecy and guaranteed returns are the big four. A routine statement in your own bank app is normal.

steps.title: Common scams to know
steps.body:
- **Fake job / check scam**: you 'get hired', receive a check, and are told to buy equipment or send part back. The check bounces days later; you are out the money.
- **Bank or government imposter**: a call or text says there is fraud on your account and asks for a code or a transfer to a 'safe account'. Real banks and the IRS don't do that.
- **Online marketplace**: the seller wants payment by Zelle or another payment app before you see the item. Those payments are hard to reverse.
- **Investment / crypto**: a new online friend shows huge gains on a platform you've never heard of.

steps.prompt: You get a text: 'BANK ALERT: suspicious $480 charge. Reply YES if not you.' Then someone calls from what looks like your bank's number and asks you to read back the code just texted to you. What do you do?

options.text: Hang up, then call the number on the back of your card or open your bank's app to check.
options.feedback: Correct. Caller ID can be faked. Contact the bank through a number you already trust.

options.text: Read them the code since the caller ID matches your bank.
options.feedback: That code lets the scammer log in or approve a transfer. Banks don't call to ask for it.

options.text: Reply YES to the text to stop the charge.
options.feedback: Replying confirms your number is active and starts the scam conversation.

steps.explain: Never share one-time codes or passwords with someone who contacted you. Hang up and reach the company through a channel you looked up yourself.

steps.prompt: If a check has 'cleared' and the money shows in your account, the check can no longer bounce.
steps.explain: Banks must make deposited funds available within a few days, before they know the check is good. A fake check can be discovered weeks later, and you owe the bank the money.

steps.prompt: You realize you just sent money and your bank login to a scammer. Put your response in order.
items: Call your bank or card company right away using a trusted number and report the fraud
Change your bank and email passwords and turn on two-factor authentication
Freeze your credit at Equifax, Experian and TransUnion
Report it at ReportFraud.ftc.gov (and IdentityTheft.gov if your identity was used)
Watch your accounts and credit reports closely for the next few months
steps.explain: Speed matters most with the bank: the faster you report, the better the chance of stopping or reversing transfers. Then lock down your accounts, freeze your credit, and report.

steps.prompt: An online job offer says you're hired after a quick chat and asks you to deposit a $2,000 check, keep $300, and send $1,700 to their 'equipment vendor' by payment app. What is this?
options: A normal onboarding process for remote jobs
A fake check scam: the check will bounce and you'll owe the $1,700
Fine as long as you wait until the check clears
Only a scam if they ask for your Social Security number
steps.explain: Real employers don't send you checks to forward to vendors. When the fake check bounces, the bank takes the full amount back from you.

steps.title: Key takeaways
steps.body:
- Pressure + secrecy + unusual payment = scam.
- Never share passwords or one-time codes with someone who contacted you.
- Hang up and call back using a number you look up.
- Turn on two-factor authentication and consider a free credit freeze.
- If it happens: call your bank first, then report at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.

steps.prompt: Agree on a 'scam rule' with your family, like a code word for real emergencies, or 'we always hang up and call back.' Write it here.
